title: DOHF: Online Diffusion Fine-tuning with Doob’s ℎ-transform Guidance

paper.title: DOHF : Online Diffusion Fine-tuning with Doob’s h h -transform Guidance
paper.abstract: Abstract Reward-based diffusion fine-tuning faces practical challenges when desirable outcomes are rare or conditioning corrections are costly to estimate. In this work, we propose Diffusion Online h h -guidance Fine-tuning (DOHF) , which turns Doob’s h h -transform into a practical online training algorithm. DOHF assigns optimality weights to generated samples, estimates the normalized local correction ∇ log ⁡ h \nabla\log h under the current rollout policy, and distills it directly into the generative model. Theoretically, we characterize the population-optimal DiffusionNFT update as well as the various classfier free guidance methods through a unified h h -transform perspective. Methodologically, our framework accommodates black-box and non-differentiable rewards without additional network evaluations. We further show improved alignments under three empirical scenarios. Our work demonstrates how adapting probabilistic conditioning through inexpensive estimation and iterative distillation can improve generative learning across statistical sampling and visual generation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Doob’s h h -transform provides a classical probabilistic mechanism for conditioning a Markov process on a terminal event or reweighting its terminal distribution ( Doob, 1957 ) . Given a terminal weight w ⁡ ( X 0 ) w(X_{0}) , the associated function h ⁡ ( x t , t ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ w ⁡ ( X 0 ) ∣ X t = x t ] h(x_{t},t)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[w(X_{0})\mid X_{t}=x_{t}ight] translates terminal information into a local correction of the intermediate dynamics through ∇ log ⁡ h 
abla\log h . This perspective has recently become increasingly relevant to diffusion models. DEFT ( Denker et al., 2024 ) formulates conditional generation through a generalized h h -transform and learns an auxiliary network. Related work studies diffusion guidance under hard constraints ( Guo et al., 2026b ) . More recently, DOIT ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) uses Doob’s h h -transform to construct a training-free adaptation procedure. From these viewpoints, a central question is how to efficiently estimate local correction for fine-tuning throughout the generative trajectory. The h h -transform gives an explicit answer. For a current rollout policy p o ​ l ​ d p^{old} and a general reward weight w w , the desired terminal distribution is p ft ​ ( x 0 ) ∝ w ⁡ ( x 0 ) ​ p o ​ l ​ d ​ ( x 0 ) , p^{\mathrm{ft}}(x_{0})\propto w(x_{0})p^{old}(x_{0}), while its intermediate score differs from that of the current model by exactly ∇ x t ​ log ​ h ​ ( x t , t ) 
abla_{x_{t}}\log h(x_{t},t) . Existing h h -transform approaches use this correction for inference-time guidance ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) , typically relative to a fixed reference model. This can become restrictive when the high-reward region is rare under the original proposal: the trajectories used to estimate the correction may provide little information precisely where adaptation is most needed. This motivates an online procedure in which the h h -function itself is defined and estimated under the evolving rollout policy, and the resulting local correction is progressively distilled into the generative model. In this work, we propose Diffusion Online h h -guidance Fine-tuning (DOHF) . At each iteration, samples from the current rollout policy are assigned an optimality weight w ⁡ ( X 0 ) w(X_{0}) , from which we estimate the corresponding ∇ log ⁡ h 
abla\log h and distill the resulting correction directly into the generative model. This online procedure progressively shifts the rollout distribution toward more informative regions, while our simulation-based estimator remains applicable to black-box and non-differentiable rewards. The same formulation naturally accommodates continuous rewards, hard or soft constraints, and relative optimality objectives. We further establish a precise connection to DiffusionNFT ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , showing when its population-optimal velocity coincides with the exact h h -transformed update. We evaluate DOHF on rare-mode adaptation, constrained contingency-table generation, and SD3.5-Medium text-to-image fine-tuning. Across these settings, DOHF consistently benefits from jointly adapting the rollout distribution and the h h -correction, leading to faster adaptation and strong reward alignment when high-reward regions are poorly represented by the original model. In conclusion, The key of DOHF is not the use of Doob’s h h -transform itself, but turning its normalized local correction into an online, self-improving training target: the correction is re-estimated under the evolving rollout policy and distilled into the model that generates the next round of data.

sections.heading: Our main contributions are:
sections.text: • Optimality as an unified framework. We formulate reward-based fine-tuning through a single weight w : 𝒳 → [ 0 , 1 ] w:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] interpreted as the probability of an optimality event { O = 1 } \{O=1\} . Exponential tilting, hard constraints w = 𝟏 { r ≥ z } w=\mathbf{1}\{r\geq z\} , their smooth relaxations, and relative optimality objectives all become instances of one object, and each induces the exact target p ft ∝ w ​ p old p^{\mathrm{ft}}\propto w\,p^{\mathrm{old}} . In contrast to formulations built on scalar advantages or on a positive/negative split of a rollout group, this retains the full conditioning structure, and in particular accommodates indicator-type hard constraints. • Online h h -guidance distillation. We turn the terminal weight into a local velocity correction − t 1 − t ​ ∇ x ​ log ⁡ h -\tfrac{t}{1-t}\nabla_{x}\log h and regress it directly into the generative model, re-estimating h h under the evolving rollout policy at every iteration. Our simulation-based estimator reuses the velocity already computed at the current step, so leads to no additional network evaluations, and w w need not be differentiable. Estimating h h and improving the rollout distribution are two sides of one update: each iteration re-collects trajectories under the tilted policy, so the correction is estimated where adaptation is most needed. • An explicit h h yields the guidance strength others must tune. We provide a population-level characterization of DiffusionNFT, showing that its update is an h h -attenuated version of the exact h h -transform and becomes exact only under the state-dependent choice β = 2 ​ h ​ ( x t , t , c ) \beta=2h(x_{t},t,c) . Since DOHF estimates h h explicitly, it realizes this state-dependent strength, whereas methods that do not must leave β \beta a constant — which attenuates the update exactly in the low- h h regions where high-reward mass is rare. We verify this prediction and the framework as a whole on rare-mode adaptation, constrained contingency-table generation, and SD3.5-M text-to-image fine-tuning, where our formulation is additionally compatible with classifier-free guidance, a design not available to forward-matching baselines.

sections.heading: Related Work.
sections.text: Existing h h -transform methods provide foundations for our work. DEFT ( Denker et al., 2024 ) , hard-constraint guidance ( Guo et al., 2026b ) , and Doob’s Matching ( Chang et al., 2026 ) learn conditioning corrections, while DOIT ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) estimates them through simulation. SVDD ( Li et al., 2024 ) , twisted SMC ( Wu et al., 2024 ) , and Feynman-Kac steering ( Singhal et al., 2025 ) offer related inference-time approaches. Tilt Matching ( Potaptchik et al., 2025 ) , Iterative Tilting ( Pachebat et al., 2025 ) , and Iterative Importance Fine-tuning ( Denker et al., 2026 ) connects tilted distributions with iterative learning. In parallel, a rapidly growing literature studies reward-based fine-tuning of diffusion models ( Uehara et al., 2024 ; Winata et al., 2025 ) . Policy-based approaches formulate the reverse generation process as a policy and optimize it through RL, including DDPO ( Black et al., 2024 ) , FlowGRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , DanceGRPO ( Xue et al., 2025 ) , DPOK ( Fan et al., 2023 ) , and MixGRPO ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Sampler stochasticity and the resulting training-inference gap are studied in ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) . ReFL ( Xu et al., 2023 ) and DRaFT ( Clark et al., 2024 ) directly differentiate reward signals, while DiffusionDPO ( Wallace et al., 2023 ) learns from preference pairs. Adjoint Matching ( Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2026a ) and Score as Action ( Zhao et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) cast fine-tuning as stochastic optimal control. Gradient-based construction ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) and flow-map alignment ( Holderrieth et al., 2026 ; Potaptchik et al., 2026 ) provide alternatives when reward derivatives are available. Regression-based approaches include Advantage Weighted Matching ( Xue et al., 2026 ) and FlowAWR ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , while online reward-weighted flow matching ( Fan et al., 2025 ) directly reweights newly generated samples. Reward Score Matching ( Lee et al., 2026 ) , a path-space perspective ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , and reward-based velocity matching ( Choi et al., 2026 ) clarify the shared structure of these updates.

sections.text: We consider contingency-table generation as an application of endogenous conditional sampling under the framework of Guo et al. (2026b) . sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced DOHF , an online diffusion fine-tuning framework based on Doob’s h h -transform. Our method turns reward-based adaptation into a local score or velocity correction that can be estimated online and directly distilled into the generative model. This perspective provides a unified treatment of continuous rewards, hard and soft constraints, and relative optimality objectives, while also clarifying the connection to existing methods such as DiffusionNFT. Across rare-mode adaptation, constrained contingency table generation, and text-to-image fine-tuning, DOHF consistently demonstrates the benefit of adapting the rollout distribution together with the model, particularly when reward-relevant regions are difficult to sample via base model. These results suggest that online h h -transform fine-tuning offers a promising alternative to both inference-time guidance and trajectory-based reinforcement learning. More broadly, the framework provides a flexible interface between probabilistic conditioning and generative-model optimization, and may be useful for a wide range of problems involving rare events, structured constraints, black-box rewards, and distributional adaptation.

In this work, we propose Diffusion Online h h -guidance Fine-tuning (DOHF) , which turns Doob’s h h -transform into a practical online training algorithm. DOHF assigns optimality weights to generated samples, estimates the normalized local correction ∇ log ⁡ h 
abla\log h under the current rollout policy, and distills it directly into the generative model. Theoretically, we characterize the population-optimal DiffusionNFT update as well as the various classfier free guidance methods through a unified h h -transform perspective. Methodologically, our framework accommodates black-box and non-differentiable rewards without additional network evaluations. We further show improved alignments under three empirical scenarios. Our work demonstrates how adapting probabilistic conditioning through inexpensive estimation and iterative distillation can improve generative learning across statistical sampling and visual generation. 1 Introduction Doob’s h h -transform provides a classical probabilistic mechanism for conditioning a Markov process on a terminal event or reweighting its terminal distribution ( Doob, 1957 ) . Given a terminal weight w ⁡ ( X 0 ) w(X_{0}) , the associated function h ⁡ ( x t , t ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ w ⁡ ( X 0 ) ∣ X t = x t ] h(x_{t},t)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[w(X_{0})\mid X_{t}=x_{t}ight] translates terminal information into a local correction of the intermediate dynamics through ∇ log ⁡ h 
abla\log h . This perspective has recently become increasingly relevant to diffusion models. DEFT ( Denker et al., 2024 ) formulates conditional generation through a generalized h h -transform and learns an auxiliary network. Related work studies diffusion guidance under hard constraints ( Guo et al., 2026b ) . More recently, DOIT ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) uses Doob’s h h -transform to construct a training-free adaptation procedure. From these viewpoints, a central question is how to efficiently estimate local correction for fine-tuning throughout the generative trajectory. The h h -transform gives an explicit answer. For a current rollout policy p o ​ l ​ d p^{old} and a general reward weight w w , the desired terminal distribution is p ft ​ ( x 0 ) ∝ w ⁡ ( x 0 ) ​ p o ​ l ​ d ​ ( x 0 ) , p^{\mathrm{ft}}(x_{0})\propto w(x_{0})p^{old}(x_{0}), while its intermediate score differs from that of the current model by exactly ∇ x t ​ log ​ h ​ ( x t , t ) 
abla_{x_{t}}\log h(x_{t},t) . Existing h h -transform approaches use this correction for inference-time guidance ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) , typically relative to a fixed reference model. This can become restrictive when the high-reward region is rare under the original proposal: the trajectories used to estimate the correction may provide little information precisely where adaptation is most needed. This motivates an online procedure in which the h h -function itself is defined and estimated under the evolving rollout policy, and the resulting local correction is progressively distilled into the generative model. In this work, we propose Diffusion Online h h -guidance Fine-tuning (DOHF) . At each iteration, samples from the current rollout policy are assigned an optimality weight w ⁡ ( X 0 ) w(X_{0}) , from which we estimate the corresponding ∇ log ⁡ h 
abla\log h and distill the resulting correction directly into the generative model. This online procedure progressively shifts the rollout distribution toward more informative regions, while our simulation-based estimator remains applicable to black-box and non-differentiable rewards. The same formulation naturally accommodates continuous rewards, hard or soft constraints, and relative optimality objectives. We further establish a precise connection to DiffusionNFT ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , showing when its population-optimal velocity coincides with the exact h h -transformed update. We evaluate DOHF on rare-mode adaptation, constrained contingency-table generation, and SD3.5-Medium text-to-image fine-tuning. Across these settings, DOHF consistently benefits from jointly adapting the rollout distribution and the h h -correction, leading to faster adaptation and strong reward alignment when high-reward regions are poorly represented by the original model. In conclusion, The key of DOHF is not the use of Doob’s h h -transform itself, but turning its normalized local correction into an online, self-improving training target: the correction is re-estimated under the evolving rollout policy and distilled into the model that generates the next round of data. Bold : best; Underline : second best. 5 Conclusion We introduced DOHF , an online diffusion fine-tuning framework based on Doob’s h h -transform. Our method turns reward-based adaptation into a local score or velocity correction that can be estimated online and directly distilled into the generative model. This perspective provides a unified treatment of continuous rewards, hard and soft constraints, and relative optimality objectives, while also clarifying the connection to existing methods such as DiffusionNFT. Across rare-mode adaptation, constrained contingency table generation, and text-to-image fine-tuning, DOHF consistently demonstrates the benefit of adapting the rollout distribution together with the model, particularly when reward-relevant regions are difficult to sample via base model. These results suggest that online h h -transform fine-tuning offers a promising alternative to both inference-time guidance and trajectory-based reinforcement learning. More broadly, the framework provides a flexible interface between probabilistic conditioning and generative-model optimization, and may be useful for a wide range of problems involving rare events, structured constraints, black-box rewards, and distributional adaptation.
